subject: Social Science
central_question: Why must India conserve its biodiversity, and how can laws, forest classification and community participation protect forests and wildlife?
in_scope_units: Flora and Fauna in India: biodiversity, ecological interdependence and the importance of forests in life-support systems.
Conservation of Forest and Wildlife in India: legal protection, national parks, sanctuaries and species-focused programmes.
Project Tiger: causes of tiger decline, the purpose of the campaign and examples of tiger reserves.
Types and Distribution of Forest and Wildlife Resources: reserved, protected and unclassed forests and their regional distribution.
Community and Conservation: village action, movements, ecological farming, sacred groves and joint forest management.
banned_topics: Detailed natural vegetation types and climatic controls from the Natural Vegetation and Wildlife chapter.
Detailed mining methods and mineral distribution from Minerals and Energy Resources.
General water scarcity and dam management from Water Resources.

known_pitfalls.claim: Biodiversity means only the number of wild animals in a region.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter defines biodiversity as the rich variety of wildlife and cultivated species, diverse in form and function, linked through networks of interdependence.

known_pitfalls.claim: Project Tiger was launched only to increase tiger numbers.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter presents tiger conservation both as protection of an endangered species and as a means of preserving large biotypes and habitats.

known_pitfalls.claim: Unclassed forests belong only to private individuals.
known_pitfalls.correction: Unclassed forests include forests and wastelands belonging to governments, private individuals and communities.

known_pitfalls.claim: Community participation is separate from formal forest conservation.
known_pitfalls.correction: Examples such as Sariska, Chipko, sacred groves and JFM show that community participation is central to conservation and restoration.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Exercise 3(i) to define biodiversity and connect it with air, water, soil and human survival.
Use NCERT Exercise 1(i) to distinguish direct community participation from formal demarcation of sanctuaries.
Use NCERT Exercise 2 to compare reserved, protected and unclassed forests.
Use NCERT Exercise 4(i) to organise evidence on community-led conservation.
Use NCERT Exercise 4(ii) to synthesise good conservation practices.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with the section “EXERCISES”, Questions 1 to 4, covering MCQ, matching, short-answer and long-answer responses.
